data.title: Pennsylvania confirms eighth measles-linked death this year
data.description:
Pennsylvania health officials have confirmed the state's eighth measles-associated death this year, a day after the U.S. officially lost its measles elimination status that was in place since 2000.

The Pennsylvania Department of Health on Wednesday said an unvaccinated resident of Clinton County tested positive for measles and died. 

Pennsylvania has been remains the hardest hit by the ongoing measles outbreak, with 1,589 confirmed cases across 46 counties so far in 2026. Just five of the reported cases were vaccinated individuals.

State officials reiterated that the best protection against measles is to be fully vaccinated. The MMR vaccine — manufactured primarily by Merck (MRK) and GlaxoSmithKline (GSK) — provides 97% lifetime protection. 

While death from measles is rare, it does occur in one to three patients per 1,000 cases.

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. blamed the COVID-19 pandemic for disrupting routine childhood vaccination.

"The multi-year global outbreak has caused many nations to lose their [measles] elimination status including, Armenia, Austria, Azerbaijan, Bolivia, Canada, Mexico, Spain, United Kingdom, and Uzbekistan," he posted on X. "We are working to close vaccination gaps and rebuild public trust."

data.title: Elanco sets $600M stock buyback plan
data.description:
• Elanco Animal Health (ELAN) said its board of directors has authorized the repurchase of up to $600M of the company's common stock.
  • The authorization reflects Elanco's accelerating operational momentum, robust free cash flow generation, strengthened balance sheet and clear path to net leverage ratio of 2.0 to 2.5 times, the company said.
  • After reaching the targeted sub 3.0x net leverage ratio, the company is updating its capital allocation priorities. Elanco will remain focused on a combination of debt paydown and accretive growth opportunities including continued investment in innovation, while starting a multi-year share repurchase program to drive enhanced, long-term shareholder value.

data.title: Trump suggests Nvidia's Blackwell chips could go to China later
data.description:
U.S. President Donald Trump said Washington could eventually permit Nvidia (NVDA) to sell its highly sought-after Blackwell chips to China once they are no longer among the most advanced processors available on the market.

“In two years or three years, I would, if I were here, I would say, go ahead. You can now sell Blackwells because they’ll have something else,” Trump said in an interview with Fox News from Shenzhen, China, where he is attending the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.

Nvidia (NVDA), according to the company's interim CEO, has stopped shipping powerful artificial intelligence chips to China, raising doubts about the future of a special licensing agreement negotiated by Washington and Beijing. But she said there were no current plans for further shipments.

Colette Kress, who succeeded Jensen Huang following his resignation last week, said on Tuesday's earnings call that Nvidia sold $2.4B in licensed Hopper-generation data centre products to China during the quarter ended October 25. Nvidia's revenue surged by 103% YoY to $115.8B, driven by sustained Blackwell demand and the speedy ramp of its Vera Rubin platform.

China's access to advanced AI chips is said to have emerged as a key point of contention at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.

data.title: Lone Pine, Viking build Alphabet stakes; Tiger cuts
data.description:
Hedge fund holdings in Alphabet (GOOGL) (GOOG) saw notable changes in the third quarter, with Lone Pine Capital significantly increasing its stake, while Tiger Global, Third Point, and Appaloosa Management were among the prominent investors who reduced their exposure, according to the latest institutional ownership disclosures.

Steve Mandel's Lone Pine Capital increased its Class A stake to 2.16 million shares from 216,000, while Andreas Halvorsen's Viking Global established a 1.73 million-share position.

Robert Soros' Soros Capital also initiated a new position with ~29,000 shares. Douglas Silverman's Senator Investment Group raised its Class C holdings to 116,000 shares from 10,000.

Meanwhile, Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway maintained substantial exposure to Alphabet, holding 78.79 million Class A shares and 27.19 million Class C shares. George Soros' Soros Fund Management also retained a significant Class A position of approximately 601,000 shares.

On the selling side, Chase Coleman's Tiger Global reduced its Class A holdings to 3.35 million shares from 5.81 million, while Dan Loeb's Third Point cut its position to 175,000 shares from 1.03 million. David Tepper's Appaloosa Management lowered its Class C stake to 1 million shares from 1.85 million, while Seth Klarman's Baupost Group reduced its holdings to 950,000 shares from 1.37 million.

Other notable moves included Dan Sundheim's D1 Capital Partners, which exited its positions in Alphabet, and Rob Citrone's Discovery Capital, which reduced its holdings to approximately 10,000 shares.

Stanley Druckenmiller's Duquesne Family Office, Brad Gerstner's Altimeter Capital and John Paulson's Paulson & Co. exited their previously reported Class A positions of 336,000, 175,000 and 5,000 shares, respectively.

The latest disclosures highlight contrasting investment strategies among major institutional investors, with some managers building exposure to Alphabet while others scale back positions or exit entirely.

data.title: World can manage without Strait of Hormuz, but no return to pre-war normal - IEA
data.description:
The world can manage without the Strait of Hormuz, but it's unlikely that energy markets can return to where they were before the start of the Iran war, according to the International Energy Agency's head Fatih Birol.

"I don't see any credible pathway back to the situation that existed in Feb. 2026," he wrote in an article for The Economist. "Confidence in the strait as a safe and reliable corridor for energy and other goods has been crushed."

As a result, countries will pay more attention to diversification. "They will pursue a more varied mix of fuels and energy technologies, of suppliers and trade routes," Birol stated. "Those new routes will include pipelines out of the Middle East that bypass Hormuz (the UAE and Saudi Arabia are already moving ahead rapidly on these)."

But while the global energy system can diversify away from the strait over time, he insisted the Middle East will remain vital for energy security and markets.

Birol's statements come as the IEA released The World Energy Outlook 2026 on Thursday, which referred to the Strait of Hormuz disruptions as the world's largest energy supply shock.

"At its peak, global oil supply fell by 16M barrels per day and gas supply by 320 million cubic meters per day," it noted.

Its report found that new bypass pipelines, alternative supplies and measures to displace demand could reduce the need for oil flows through the strait from 20 mb/d before the crisis to 8.5 mb/d in 2030 and to under 2 mb/d by 2035.

"But even in this extreme case, the Middle East would remain the world's largest exporter of oil to international markets," the report affirmed.

Notably, Goldman Sachs expects an additional 3.8 mb/d of pipeline capacity to come online over the next year as Middle East oil producers invest in pipelines that bypass the Strait of Hormuz and transport directly to the Gulf of Oman, Red Sea or Mediterranean Sea.
